# Why

`PostToolUse` hooks can already inspect the stable `tool_response` that Codex exposes after a tool runs, but they cannot currently replace the result that the model sees on the next turn. Supporting the existing `updatedToolOutput` / `updatedMCPToolOutput` hook fields lets hook authors redact or normalize direct model-visible tool output without mutating the underlying typed tool result.

That distinction matters for code mode: nested tools can be chained together inside a running program, so rewriting an intermediate value would change program behavior and break the caller's expectation about what the previous tool actually returned.

# What

- parse `updatedToolOutput` and/or `updatedMCPToolOutput` from `PostToolUse` hook output
  - `updatedToolOutput` takes precedence over `updatedMCPToolOutput`
- validate replacements by JSON kind against the original hook-facing `tool_response`; invalid replacements are ignored with a hook warning
- preserve the original typed `ToolOutput` while applying accepted replacements only to the direct model-visible response item
- keep code-mode nested tool results unchanged, so code mode continues to receive original structured outputs while direct model calls can see the rewritten projection
- cover the split with direct shell/MCP rewrite tests, invalid-shape coverage, and a code-mode regression that proves nested `exec_command` output is not rewritten

# Documentation

The public hook spec should document that `updatedToolOutput` / `updatedMCPToolOutput` affect the model-visible projection only and do not rewrite code-mode intermediate results.

## Why

Codex users often work across several Git worktrees while keeping each session tied to a specific branch, checkout, and pending-change state. Until now, the CLI/TUI did not have a first-class workflow for that: users had to create raw Git worktrees themselves, the TUI did not make worktree transitions visible, and cleanup had no Codex ownership boundary.

This PR adds a managed worktree workflow for Codex-created worktrees while still respecting ordinary Git worktrees. CLI-created worktrees use predictable sibling paths, App-created worktrees remain discoverable, and Codex refuses to remove worktrees it does not own.

## What Changed

- Added a new `codex-worktree` crate that owns managed worktree lifecycle behavior:
  - create or reuse sibling worktrees from the default base or an explicit base ref;
  - preserve the relative cwd when starting from a repo subdirectory;
  - store Codex ownership and thread metadata beside Git worktree metadata;
  - list CLI-managed, App-managed, legacy, and raw Git worktrees distinctly;
  - refuse removal of worktrees that are not Codex-managed.
- Added CLI entry points for startup and lifecycle management:
  - `--worktree <BRANCH>`
  - `--worktree-base <REF>`
  - `--worktree-dirty <MODE>`
  - `codex worktree list|path|remove|prune`
- Added the TUI `/worktree` workflow for creating, switching, locating, and removing worktrees.
  - The picker shows an animated loading/progress state while helper work is running.
  - Creating a worktree asks only for the branch name and uses the default base.
  - If the source checkout is dirty, the interactive flow asks whether to move all pending changes or leave them in place.
  - Power users can still use explicit slash/CLI flags for base refs and granular dirty policies.
- Added workspace labels in startup, resume, fork, and status surfaces so sessions make their worktree context visible.
- Added app-server-backed workspace command execution so the same `/worktree` flow works for embedded and remote TUI sessions.
- Made dirty transfers safer:
  - tracked patches preserve exact diff output;
  - failed creates roll back newly-created worktrees and branches;
  - move policies clean the source only after the destination has been populated safely.

## How to Test

1. From a Git repo, start Codex in a managed sibling worktree:
   ```sh
   cargo run --bin codex -- --worktree fcoury/worktree-smoke --worktree-dirty ignore
   ```
2. Confirm the session starts in a sibling path such as `../codex.fcoury-worktree-smoke`.
3. Run:
   ```sh
   cargo run --bin codex -- worktree list
   cargo run --bin codex -- worktree path fcoury/worktree-smoke
   ```
   Confirm the list distinguishes Codex-managed entries from raw Git worktrees.
4. In the TUI, run `/worktree` and confirm the picker shows a loading spinner before the list appears.
5. Choose `New worktree...`, enter only a branch name, and confirm no base-ref prompt appears.
6. Start from a dirty checkout, create a worktree, choose `Move changes`, and confirm tracked changes and untracked files move into the new worktree while the source checkout is left clean.
7. Re-open `/worktree`, select the current row, and confirm Codex reports that you are already in that worktree.
8. Try removing a raw Git worktree from the list and confirm Codex refuses because it is not Codex-managed.
9. For remote coverage, connect a TUI session with `--remote` and repeat the create/switch flow; confirm the session switches to the remote worktree cwd and the helper output remains JSON-clean.

Targeted tests:
- `cargo test -p codex-worktree`
- `cargo test -p codex-tui worktree`

## Documentation

This adds user-facing CLI flags, `codex worktree` subcommands, and the TUI `/worktree` workflow. The Codex CLI documentation on developers.openai.com should be updated before this ships broadly.

# Summary

Queued follow-up turns currently live in clients. If a renderer reloads or a client disconnects before it submits the next follow-up, that future turn can disappear before app-server ever sees it.

This PR adds the app-server-owned backend primitive for durable queued turns. App-server now stores queued future turns, exposes an experimental `thread/queue/*` JSON-RPC surface, emits queue snapshots, and drains the next queued turn when the thread becomes idle. The stored payload is the original `TurnStartParams`, so queued dispatch uses the same turn-start shape that direct `turn/start` already accepts.

This PR stays backend-focused. It does not migrate Codex App or TUI queue ownership yet; it creates the server contract those client follow-ups can move onto next.

# What changed

- Added experimental v2 queue RPCs and notifications:
  - `thread/queue/add`
  - `thread/queue/list`
  - `thread/queue/delete`
  - `thread/queue/reorder`
  - `thread/queue/changed`
- Added durable SQLite queue rows backed by serialized `TurnStartParams` JSONB/BLOB payloads.
- Added app-server queue processing for add/list/delete/reorder, visible queue snapshots, dispatch claiming, failure marking, and restart recovery of interrupted dispatch claims.
- Reused the existing app-server turn-start path for queued dispatch instead of inventing a parallel runnable-turn construction path.
- Triggered queue drain after idle adds, terminal turn events, and thread resume/recovery.
- Updated generated app-server schemas/types, app-server docs, and the tiny TUI notification exhaustiveness sites affected by the new notification variant.

# Design decisions

- The queue payload is serialized `TurnStartParams`. `thread_id` stays indexed on the queue row and remains inside the payload so dispatch can deserialize the exact future turn that was queued.
- Public queue state is `pending` or `failed`. The short-lived `dispatching` state is internal coordination state and is never rendered to clients.
- Selecting the head row for dispatch is the queue commit point. Once a row is claimed, concurrent delete/reorder requests only operate on still-visible queue rows.
- A failed head row blocks FIFO draining until the client removes or reorders queue state. The server does not silently skip failed work.
- App-server owns durable queue state and dispatch. Core continues to receive ordinary turn starts through the existing thread path.
- Queue and steer remain separate product operations. This PR does not ask app-server to infer what the user meant.

# Important call sites

| Area | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `app-server-protocol` | Add generated queue request/response/notification types and experimental method registration. |
| `state` | Add durable queued-turn rows plus append, visible list, delete, reorder, claim, fail, remove, and recovery operations. |
| `app-server` queue processor | Own validation, snapshots, dispatch drain, dispatch failure state, and restart recovery. |
| `turn_processor` | Reuse app-server turn-start validation/start behavior for deserialized queued payloads. |
| thread lifecycle | Drain after terminal turn events and resume queue snapshots after recovery. |
| docs/tests | Document the API and cover serialized dispatch, busy-thread mutations, dispatch races, failed-head blocking, and interrupted-claim recovery. |

# Testing

Tests: targeted app-server queue integration coverage, queued-turn state/race coverage, app-server protocol coverage, full TUI coverage for the notification exhaustiveness touch, schema regeneration, scoped Clippy autofix, and staged diff whitespace validation.

Smoke tests: terminal/API smoke covering real `thread/queue/add`, `list`, `reorder`, `delete`, and `thread/queue/changed` traffic; state-concurrency smoke covering claim/recovery/failure ordering; Linux desktop smoke proving the rebuilt Codex CLI can be launched through Codex Desktop on the devbox display.

# Visual evidence

Visual smoke artifacts were recaptured locally for the new app-server-focused head. Inline GitHub attachments will be added to this section once the PR attachment upload path is completed from the devbox session.

## Why

`conversation_webrtc_close_while_sideband_connecting_drops_pending_join` was flaky on slow CI because the mocked sideband handshake could finish before the close path aborted the pending join task. When that race wins, the test observes the wrong event sequence even though the product behavior is unchanged.

Failure evidence: [remote Ubuntu test job](https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/26116725532/job/76807810858) with uploaded [nextest JUnit artifact](https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/26116725532/artifacts/7092348148)

## What changed

- keep the mocked sideband accept delayed past the stale-event observation window
- make websocket mock shutdown interrupt that delay so the test does not pay a fixed multi-second teardown tail
- make the close-while-connecting case deterministic instead of scheduler-sensitive

## CI evidence

Recent failed `rust-ci-full` test runs that exposed this flake family:
- https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/26115775739

`/review` threads could surface an MCP elicitation prompt in the parent UI, but the user’s response was then submitted to the parent session. The pending elicitation responder actually lived in the delegated child session, so resolution failed with elicitation request not found and the `/review` remained blocked as if the user never responded.

This change handles delegated MCP elicitation events in the delegate bridge: it asks through the parent session/UI, then relays the resolved response back to the child session. It also routes delegated elicitations through unique parent-side request IDs so concurrent child-local request IDs do not collide. Per codex feedback, an additional change was made to retain auto-deny behavior in Xcode 26.4 clients. Added regression coverage for delegate-bridge forwarding, parent-session round-trip back to the child, and parent-side request ID namespacing.

## Implementation Changes

Roughly 25% of this PR is production code in the delegate bridge, while about 75% is delegate unit test coverage for the delegated MCP elicitation round trip and parent-side request ID namespacing.

- Modified delegate bridge behavior
  - `codex_delegate` now intercepts delegated `ElicitationRequest` events instead of letting them fall through as ordinary child events.
  - The bridge converts the child-local elicitation payload into a parent-session MCP elicitation request, so the existing parent UI/session path owns prompting the user.
  - After the parent session resolves the prompt, the bridge relays that decision, content, and metadata back to the delegated child with `Op::ResolveElicitation`.
  - Delegated elicitation cancellation is handled explicitly: if the delegate bridge is cancelled while the parent prompt is pending, the parent-side pending request is resolved as cancelled and the child receives a cancelled response.
  - Invalid delegated elicitation payloads are treated as a child-side cancel rather than leaving the delegate blocked.
  - Existing Xcode 26.4 auto-deny behavior is preserved by short-circuiting delegated elicitations when the parent MCP manager is configured to auto-deny.

- Modified request ID routing
  - Delegated MCP elicitation request IDs are now namespaced at the parent boundary by minting a unique parent-side request ID.
  - The child’s original request ID is retained only for the final response back to that child.
  - This prevents collisions if multiple delegated children emit the same child-local MCP request ID concurrently.
  - This is not a major concern given the current use of delegation via /review mode, but Codex kept flagging it as an issue and it was too simple to not include this in these changes.

- New regression coverage
  - Added focused delegate unit tests covering:
     - forwarding a child ElicitationRequest through the delegate bridge into the parent event stream and relaying the parent response back to the child
     - direct parent-session elicitation round-trip back to the delegated child
     - unique parent-side request ID routing when concurrent children reuse the same child-local MCP request ID


## Testing/Duplicating the bug
In order to test this, you must configure an MCP server that emits elicitations and ensure that the review agent calls this server during a code review. I achieved this by having Codex create a simple MCP server/tool combination that emits elicitations, and edited AGENTS.md in a repo with instructions that this specific MCP tool call must be performed at the start of a `/review`. I then used `/review`, and confirmed the thread did not get stuck after the elicitation was approved.

When tested against the current Codex release, after the elicitation was accepted the thread was stuck. This occurs because the elicitation response was submitted to the parent session instead of the delegated child, so the child remained blocked.

## Why

The app-server can host multiple clients in the same long-lived process, but client identity was still largely process-global. That made attribution fragile: one initialized client could influence outbound `originator` and `User-Agent` headers for later app-server work, while infrastructure clients such as `codex_app_server_daemon` and `codex-backend` were excluded from global mutation even when they initiated session work.

Model/realtime requests, telemetry, and connector filtering should use the client identity for the connection that owns the request, not whatever process-global identity happens to be set.

## What Changed

- Added a scoped `ClientIdentity` path in `codex-login` that can build originator, `User-Agent`, default headers, and reqwest clients from an explicit identity while preserving existing process-default behavior outside the scope.
- Changed app-server `initialize` to validate and store a concrete identity for every initialized connection, including daemon/backend clients, without mutating process-global originator or user-agent suffix.
- Wrapped initialized app-server request handling, including background thread-start work, in the connection's scoped identity so async downstream work sees the right client.
- Updated `ModelClient` and realtime paths to use the scoped/session identity for HTTP requests, Responses websocket handshakes, realtime call creation, and sideband/default headers.
- Threaded the per-turn originator through telemetry, connector/app-tool filtering, MCP skill dependency checks, and plugin-install discovery paths so those decisions no longer depend on process-global identity.

## Verification

- Added `codex-login` coverage for scoped identity overriding process-default headers.
- Added app-server coverage for a multi-connection websocket regression where `codex-backend` initializes first and a later `codex_ios` thread still sends model requests with `codex_ios` headers.
- Updated initialize coverage so daemon/backend-style clients receive explicit connection-scoped user agents and explicit initialize identity ignores `CODEX_INTERNAL_ORIGINATOR_OVERRIDE`.

## Why

Code-mode can truncate its final `exec` result after a nested tool result has already been shortened. When that happens, the only truncation clue may be buried inside the output body, which makes it easy for the model to miss that the code-mode result itself lost content.

## What

- Thread code-mode truncation metadata into the script status header.
- Add a top-level warning when the final code-mode output is truncated.
- Keep generic unified exec formatting unchanged.
- Update code-mode truncation coverage for direct `exec` output and `wait` output.

Before, outer code-mode truncation was only visible inside the body:

I like to keep `model_reasoning_summary` enabled for models like `gpt-5.5`, but I hit a hard 400 when switching to a model such as `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` that rejects `reasoning.summary`. That makes a global config value block model switching.

## Why

Pending input was split across multiple places: turn-local pending input in `TurnState`, next-turn response items in `InputQueue`, and mailbox input that had to be folded in separately. That made the turn lifecycle harder to reason about, especially around aborts, empty active turns, and the handoff from a finished turn to queued follow-up work.

This PR merges pending turn input into one session-owned queue in `InputQueue`, so pending work has a single owner and a single drain path.

## What changed

- Remove `TurnInputQueue` and the `TurnState` pending-input field.
- Replace the separate idle response-item queue with one `InputQueueState::turn_pending_input` list.
- Store pending items as `TurnInput`, so the shared queue can hold either steered `UserInput` or raw `ResponseInputItem`s.
- Collapse enqueueing onto `InputQueue::inject` and delete the next-turn response-item queue helpers.
- Drain pending input directly from `InputQueue` during `run_turn`, alongside eligible mailbox input.
- Remove finish-time pending-input re-injection; queued work is handled by the normal pending-work wakeup path.
- Keep the existing behavior that only `TurnInput::UserInput` runs user-prompt hooks and emits user-message lifecycle items.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p codex-core`
- `git diff --check`

## Documentation

No developer documentation updates are needed.

Once HTTP identity is explicit, app-server work needs to use the identity for the connection that owns the request. Otherwise one initialized client can still affect later session, model, and realtime work in the same long-lived process.

## Why

Several Windows reports show Codex TUI control sequences being rendered as visible text instead of being interpreted by the terminal. The affected startup shapes are still not fully pinned down: [#23512](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23512) narrows one report to repo-conditioned startup, while [#23031](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23031) and [#23628](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23628) show the same raw-control-byte symptom in other startup contexts.

The boundary we can harden now is smaller and concrete. When Windows stdout is an inspectable console handle and VT processing is still disabled, raw ANSI-only TUI extras should not emit OSC, synchronized-update, alternate-screen, or inline-history control bytes into the user-visible terminal buffer.

## What Changed

- Added shared Windows stdout VT inspection and enable/verify helpers in [`codex-terminal-detection`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/364c3fbe219b60ffb6dbd888edc2db7f14448e79/codex-rs/terminal-detection/src/lib.rs).
- Added a single TUI raw-ANSI capability gate in [`tui/src/raw_ansi.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/364c3fbe219b60ffb6dbd888edc2db7f14448e79/codex-rs/tui/src/raw_ansi.rs).
- Verify the Windows stdout VT state before optional startup mode writes, and skip raw ANSI-only title, synchronized-update, alternate-screen, and inline-history paths when inspectable stdout cannot be brought to a VT-enabled state.
- Preserve existing behavior for stdout handles that cannot be inspected as Windows console handles, so PTY-style paths do not get treated as broken just because console-mode visibility is unavailable.
- Extend the existing `codex doctor` terminal details with Windows stdout console-mode visibility and VT-processing state without mutating terminal mode during the doctor run.

When Codex has to degrade, the TUI keeps running on the safer paths and keeps transcript state in the app. The terminal scrollback/history insertion extras are the part that get skipped while Windows stdout VT output is not trustworthy.

## How to Test

1. On Windows Terminal, run `codex doctor --json`.
2. Confirm the existing `terminal.env` details include Windows stdout console-mode visibility plus Windows stdout VT-processing state.
3. Start Codex from a Git repo and confirm the startup card and composer render normally without literal control-byte text such as `ESC]0`, `ESC[?2026h`, or scroll-region escape output.
4. Start Codex from a directory outside a Git repo and confirm the normal startup path still renders normally.
5. For the disabled-VT path, use a local harness that forces inspectable Windows stdout VT processing off, then confirm Codex skips raw ANSI-only extras instead of printing title, synchronized-update, or inline-history control bytes. This PR intentionally does not add a production flag for that forced-failure path.

Targeted tests:
- `cargo test -p codex-tui raw_ansi`
- `cargo test -p codex-cli terminal_check_reports`
- `cargo test -p codex-terminal-detection`

## Summary

The feedback uploader currently queues a Sentry envelope through the default Rust SDK transport and then calls `flush()`. That only proves the transport worker drained its queue; HTTP 413/429 and network failures are logged at debug level by the SDK and are not surfaced to callers. As a result `/feedback` can show a successful feedback/thread ID even when ingest rejected the envelope.

This changes the feedback upload path to serialize the envelope and POST it synchronously to the DSN envelope endpoint, returning an error for transport failures or non-2xx ingest statuses. It also canonicalizes legacy webview `bad-result`/`good-result` classifications to the underscored values used by the TUI/server so those reports are not mislabeled as Other/Info. The error includes the HTTP status and envelope byte length (with a bounded response snippet) so callers can distinguish oversized payloads/rate limits from success.

## Invariant / non-goal drift guard

A locally-created event/thread id is not an acknowledgement. The caller may report success (and show/return the id) only after the ingest endpoint has acknowledged the envelope with 2xx. Network errors, timeouts, and non-2xx responses must remain visible failures; follow-up retries/fallbacks (for example, retrying without attachments) can happen before success, but must not convert an unacknowledged upload into a "submitted" result.

## Notes

- This is intentionally scoped to the user-visible feedback upload path; it does not change general Sentry error reporting.
- Hyphenated classification aliases are accepted for backwards compatibility, but Sentry tags are written in canonical underscore form.
- The app-server already runs feedback upload in `spawn_blocking`, so the blocking request does not block the async runtime there.
- Follow-up work should likely cap/retry attachments and improve the UI label, but this PR makes false-success impossible for the current path.

## Test plan

- `cd codex-rs && RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.95.0 cargo test -p codex-feedback acknowledged_transport_tests -- --nocapture`

`codex exec resume` currently requires a prompt even when app-server resumes a thread that already has an active goal. That forces users to invent a fake prompt like `continue`, which records a user turn instead of letting goal continuation own the next turn.

Sessions without an active goal still require a prompt or piped stdin, and promptless resume now fails fast when the caller supplied images or `--output-schema`, since those inputs need a prompt-bound turn.

The resume path also handles already-running active-goal turns returned by `thread/resume`, keeps Ctrl-C active while waiting for a goal continuation turn, and bounds that wait so active goals that cannot auto-start do not hang exec.

## Why

Multi-agent behavior was selected from feature flags at multiple runtime call sites. That allowed resumed or forked threads to observe current configuration instead of the runtime they started with, and it allowed parent and child threads to disagree about which multi-agent system was active.

A thread should select its multi-agent system once and use that decision for its lifetime.

## What changed

- Add `MultiAgentVersion::{Disabled, V1, V2}` and persist it as an optional rollout `SessionMeta` field. Missing metadata means an unresolved legacy rollout; `Disabled` is an explicit locked decision.
- Resolve a session once from persisted rollout metadata, an inherited parent lock, or fresh-root feature flags. Fresh roots select `V2` when `MultiAgentV2` is enabled, otherwise `V1` when `Collab` is enabled, otherwise `Disabled`.
- Store the selected runtime in `Session` as `OnceLock<MultiAgentVersion>` and copy it into turn context. Runtime tool planning, usage hints, depth behavior, interrupted-turn markers, fork filtering, completion notifications, and descendant resume read the lock instead of feature flags.
- On a legacy resume or fork, reuse the newest matching metadata line when present. A newest null remains unresolved instead of falling through to an older value. When seeding an unresolved source rollout, clone that newest line so accumulated append-only metadata fields are preserved.

# Why

`SessionStart` hooks need a structured, shell-agnostic way to publish dynamic environment variables to subsequent local shell commands. This supports setup hooks that discover paths or configure tools without requiring environment-file parsing or cross-shell serialization.

# What

- Add `hookSpecificOutput.env` to `SessionStart` command output as a string key-value map.
- Merge values from matching `SessionStart` handlers in configured order, later handlers win for duplicate keys.
- Store the merged overlay on the session and apply it to subsequent local standalone shell commands, shell tool calls, and unified exec processes. Preserve the overlay when shell snapshots are restored.
- Inherit the parent session overlay when spawning subagents so child shell commands receive the same setup as a spawn-time snapshot.
- Reject malformed environment names, NUL-containing values, and the runtime-owned `CODEX_THREAD_ID` variable.

# Hook handler output

To publish environment variables, a `SessionStart` command hook should return JSON with an `env` object inside `hookSpecificOutput`:

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "env": {
      "PATH": "/path/to/plugin/bin:/usr/bin",
      "PLUGIN_HOME": "/path/to/plugin"
    }
  }
}
```

`env` is an optional string-to-string map. Keys must be non-empty and cannot contain `=` or NUL. Values cannot contain NUL.

The overlay applies to subsequent local shell commands in the session; it is not applied to remote execution environments.

# Why

When an organization allows only the elevated Windows sandbox, Codex prompts the user to run the elevated setup helper before continuing.

We observed a user close the running setup helper after setup had started but before it completed. The orchestrator relied on the helper process exit alone, so the TUI announced that the sandbox was ready even though only part of the on-disk setup had been initialized. Model-only turns still worked, while the first shell command detected the incomplete setup and failed closed.

This did not weaken sandbox enforcement or create a bypass, but the readiness signal was incorrect and the recovery experience was confusing.

# What

- Add a nonce-tagged setup completion report under `.sandbox-secrets`.
- Mark the report `pending` before launching each elevated setup helper, invalidating any earlier successful receipt.
- Let the helper mark that exact nonce `complete` only after every synchronous setup stage succeeds.
- Require the matching completed receipt before treating a successful helper process exit as setup success.
- Include the receipt in startup and command-time readiness checks, so partial marker/user files cannot skip setup retry.
- Bump the Windows sandbox setup version so existing installations establish the new readiness artifact once.

This deliberately uses positive proof of completion instead of trying to make every Windows termination path produce a particular exit code. Closing the helper, a crash, or another premature termination all leave the receipt pending and follow the existing required-sandbox Retry/Quit failure flow. Refresh-only ACL updates remain unchanged and do not replace the receipt.
